context: foundations-to-deck sequence · bearings & structural monitoring drive commissioning

brief.intro: A bridge or viaduct project builds a spanning structure across an obstacle — a valley, river, road or rail line — so the substructure (foundations and piers) and the superstructure (deck) dominate the programme, not building-style MEP. The critical sequence is foundations → piers → deck erection, and the erection method — balanced cantilever, incremental launch, precast segmental, or falsework-supported cast-in-place — sets a very different rate of progress for each project. Bearings and expansion joints, though structural items, are commissioning-critical: they are supplied, set and load-tested almost like mechanical equipment before the structure is accepted. Systems scope is light — feature/navigation lighting, structural-health monitoring and lightning protection/earthing — so your schedule stands or falls on the foundation and pier construction rate, the chosen deck-erection method's cycle time, and protecting the load-test and bearing-acceptance activities near the end.

scope.desc: Steel tendons stressed inside a concrete box-girder or segmental deck once cast.

scope.name: Deck furniture
scope.desc: Parapets, drainage, waterproofing and running surface.

scope.desc: Embankments and transition slabs tying the bridge into the road or rail alignment.

scope.name: Structural monitoring & lighting
scope.desc: Structural-health-monitoring sensors, lightning protection and feature/navigation lighting.

scope.name: Testing, load-proving & handover
scope.desc: Static/dynamic load test, monitoring baseline and handover to the asset owner.

must_get_right: The deck-erection method decides the whole programme rhythm — its cycle time (per segment, per push, per span) must be nailed down before the baseline is built, not assumed generic.
Foundations and piers are almost always the true critical path — the deck can't start until the piers it lands on are complete and cured.
Bearings and expansion joints are structural but commissioning-critical — protect real time for supply, setting and load-test/acceptance near the end.
Approach embankments and transition slabs must tie in cleanly with the deck ends — a mismatch here delays the whole corridor handover, not just the bridge.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The deck-erection method — balanced cantilever, incremental launch, segmental, or falsework cast-in-place — is modelled as a repeating cycle fragnet so its true cycle time drives the deck duration, not an assumed generic rate.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Foundation and substructure works run a standard 6-day calendar; marine or river piling is tide- and season-restricted where applicable. Deck-erection cycles run on a fixed cycle-time calendar — days per segment, push, or span — so the crew and plant are resourced consistently.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs foundations → piers/abutments → deck erection (by the governing method) → post-tensioning → bearings set → deck furniture/waterproofing → load test → handover. Piers must reach design strength before the deck lands on them; bearings and expansion joints, though structural, sit on the critical path into the final load test.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design and approvals, including the erection-method statement, are frozen before substructure starts; ground conditions match the geotechnical baseline report; temporary works — falsework, launching nose, segment yard — are available when needed; a single mobilisation. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The following are tracked as milestones and drive the network:

rows: Precast segments (if segmental) / launching nose (if launched)
Structural steel girders — if steel deck

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Crane and launching-gantry / segment-lifter capacity governs the deck-erection rate; access over the obstacle being crossed — river, live road, rail possession windows — restricts working hours and lift windows. Specialist stressing and bearing-setting crews are a shared, limited resource across the industry.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: ground conditions differing from the geotechnical baseline at pile or pier locations, erection-method productivity running below the planned cycle time, and load-test non-conformance requiring rework. Schedule contingency is held around the foundation-to-pier handoff and before the final load test, rather than spread across the repeating deck cycle.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client, by structure/span; controlled at Level 3, with the deck-erection cycle tracked as a repeating fragnet; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
